title: The Small-Encoder Crossover Is a Prompted-Baseline Artefact: A Fine-Tuned Encoder Head Loses to a Fine-Tuned 4B Decision Model by 0.33 and to a Majority-Class Control
content: Every public “a small encoder wins” result we were able to locate inside the target corpus compares that encoder against a prompted (zero- or few-shot) LLM, never against a fine-tuned generative decider (the claim and its audit trail are internal to the corpus, not an external survey — §2). That a fine-tuned generative decider can beat a fine-tuned encoder at comparable effort is already public— a 2025 practitioner blog post reports exactly that on a binary ADE task (§2.1) — so we claim no priority for the direction; what we claim is this fixture, its controls and its diagnosis. We measure the fine-tuned comparison on a sealed typed-single-label decision fixture. Headline. The best fine-tuned encoder head scores 0.3474 and loses to the fine-tuned 4B decider at 0.6789 — the declared primary baseline (author decision 2026-10-15), the auditable same-run arm — with paired McNemar b = 27, c = 90, ψ = 0.616, ∆ = −0.3316, exact p = 4.167e−09. The control that could have contradicted this is the mandatory majority-class control, and it did contradict the candidate’s framing of itself: majority-class returns 0.4526, beating every fine-tuned encoder head by +0.1053. The second control that could have contradicted the measurement is the shuffled-label arm, and it moved the other way from a spurious win: it returns 0.2316, below the fixture’s 0.2911 chance floor. A third control guards instrument integrity: our n-gram leak criterion (≥ 2 distinct shared 8-grams within one row pair, both directions) flagged 0 of 152,000 training↔fixture pairs — and, to show the criterion can fire, it flagged three deliberately seeded copies at 13 / 44 / 57 shared 8-grams (pair maxima). Against the published, pre-registered baseline 0.6684 — which cannot be re-scored from the tree — the same head loses by 0.3210 (“0.32”) against the secondary baseline 0.6684. The two figures use two baselines and must not be read as one: the headline 0.3316 (“0.33”) is computed against the declared primary 0.6789, while 0.3210 (“0.32”) is computed against the secondary/published 0.6684, which is the pre-registered F1 threshold and which cannot be re-scored from the tree. Correction carried. Fixing three defects lowered the SetFit-MPNet arm monotonically (0.3158 → 0.2947 → 0.2632), but the same order-probe fix raised the ModernBERT-base arm (0.342105 → 0.347368). The universal claim “every correction moved the affected arm down” is false; the SetFit arm returned the opposite direction from the ModernBERT arm, which is the control on that claim. Not in this paper. We make no latency claim: the encoder heads were timed locally in one forward batch while the 4B figures come from a served stack’s stored rows, so the tree cannot support a fair latency comparison (see §6.1). We also do not report κ = 0.9014 (first blind reader) or κ = 0.8577 (second, independent blind reader) — nor their mutual κ = 0.9125 —as inter-annotator agreement: both labellers were models, so this is machine reproducibility of the fixture, not human agreement. The second reader partially replicates the first: the κ magnitude holds (both ≥ 0.85) but the exact 0.90 headline does not. An independent human labeller is still owed (§6.2).
